title: The Greek-Script Inscriptions
subtitle: The twenty-four letters of the Massaliote alphabet and their Gaulish sounds.
objectives: Recognize all twenty-four letters of the Greek alphabet in Gaulish epigraphy.
Pronounce Gaulish words written in Greek letters.
Understand the phonetic approximations Greek scribes made for Gaulish sounds.
Read and parse a complete Greek-script votive inscription.

sections.heading: The Massaliote alphabet
sections.body: The Greeks who settled Massalia around 600 BCE brought the Ionian alphabet, the same system used in Athens and throughout the eastern Greek world by the 4th century BCE. When Gauls in the Rhône valley began writing their language in Greek letters, they used this alphabet unchanged. The result: twenty-four Greek letters pressed into service for a Celtic sound system they were not designed for.

letters.name: alpha
letters.note: Short or long a, as in Gaulish ANDEVDOS (name).

letters.name: beta
letters.note: As in Greek. Gaulish had /b/, but it was rare.

letters.name: gamma
letters.note: Always hard g. Common in Gaulish names: SEGOMĀROS (great victory).

letters.name: delta
letters.note: As in Greek. Gaulish DEDEMIT (he gave) uses this letter twice.

letters.name: epsilon
letters.note: Short e. Greek scribes used epsilon for Gaulish short /e/.

letters.name: zeta
letters.note: Rare in Gaulish. Used for names borrowed from Greek.

letters.name: eta
letters.note: Long e. Greek scribes could mark vowel length in Gaulish.

letters.name: theta
letters.note: Aspirated t. Not native to Gaulish; used in Greek loanwords.

letters.name: iota
letters.note: Short or long i.

letters.name: kappa
letters.note: Gaulish /k/. Very common.

letters.name: lambda
letters.note: As in Greek.

letters.name: mu
letters.note: Common in Gaulish. SEGOMĀROS, MĀRKOM (horse).

letters.name: nu
letters.note: As in Greek.

letters.name: xi
letters.note: Rare in Gaulish epigraphy.

letters.name: omicron
letters.note: Short o. Greek scribes used omicron for short /o/.

letters.name: pi
letters.note: Gaulish had /p/, though it was less common than /k/ or /t/.

letters.name: rho
letters.note: Gaulish /r/ was probably trilled.

letters.name: sigma
letters.note: Very common. SEGOMĀROS, ESUS (god name).

letters.name: tau
letters.note: Common. DEDEMIT, TANNACOS (thin?).

letters.name: upsilon
letters.note: Greek upsilon for Gaulish /u/. But Gaulish /u:/ was often written ΟΥ (ou).

letters.name: phi
letters.note: Aspirated p. Not native to Gaulish; used in Greek loanwords.

letters.name: chi
letters.note: Aspirated k. Not native to Gaulish; used in Greek loanwords.

letters.name: psi
letters.note: Rare in Gaulish.

letters.name: omega
letters.note: Long o. Greek scribes could distinguish short /o/ (omicron) from long /ō/ (omega) in Gaulish.

sections.heading: The problem of /u:/
sections.body: Gaulish had a long /u:/ sound that Greek did not. Greek upsilon (Υ) was pronounced /y/ (like French u or German ü) by the time of Massalia's founding. Gaulish scribes solved this by writing long /u:/ as ΟΥ (omicron + upsilon), a digraph that approximated the sound. This convention carried over into Latin-script Gaulish, where <ou> became the standard spelling for /u:/. Example: ΟΥΙΛΛΟΝΕΟΣ (Ouilloneos) = /wi:llone:os/.

sections.heading: Reading a Greek-script votive
sections.body:
Here is the complete text of a votive inscription from Vaison-la-Romaine, dating to around 100 BCE:

ΣΕΓΟΜΑΡΟΣ ΟΥΙΛΛΟΝΕΟΣ ΤΟΟΥΤΙΟΥΣ ΝΑΜΑΥΣΑΤΙΣ ΕΙΟΡΟΥ ΒΗΛΗΣΑΜΙ ΣΟΣΙΝ ΝΕΜΗΤΟΝ

Transliteration: SEGOMAROS OUILLONEOS TOOUTIOUṢ NAMAUSATIS EIORU BĒLĒSAMI SOSIN NEMĒTON

Gloss: Segomaros son of Ouillo, citizen of Nemausus (modern Nîmes), set up this sacred grove to Belisama.

Parsing: SEGOMAROS (nom. sg., personal name, "great victory"), OUILLONEOS (gen. sg., patronymic, "of Ouillo"), TOOUTIOUṢ (nom. sg., "citizen"), NAMAUSATIS (gen. sg., ethnic, "of Nemausus"), EIORU (3rd sg. aorist, "set up"), BĒLĒSAMI (dat. sg., goddess name, "to Belisama"), SOSIN (demonstrative, "this"), NEMĒTON (acc. sg., "sacred grove").

items.prompt: How many letters are in the Greek alphabet used for Gaulish?
items.answer: Twenty-four, the same as the standard Greek alphabet of the 4th century BCE.

items.prompt: Why do Greek-script Gaulish inscriptions write /u:/ as ΟΥ?
items.answer: Greek upsilon was pronounced /y/ by this period, not /u/. The digraph ΟΥ approximated the Gaulish long /u:/ sound.
"Great victory" or "victory-great" — a compound of SEGO- (victory) and -MĀROS (great).
Dative singular. The ending -i marks the dative in Gaulish -ā- stem nouns.
A sacred grove or sanctuary, a common Gaulish religious site.

items.prompt: Which three Greek letters represent sounds not native to Gaulish?
items.answer: Theta (Θ), phi (Φ), and chi (Χ) — the aspirated stops, used only in Greek loanwords.

sections.heading: Divine names in Greek script
sections.instructions: These Gaulish god names appear in Greek-script dedications. Practice reading them aloud.
